idiom_name: state owner plus published prop getters, consumer-supplied render
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: a behaviour object owns the widget's state and transitions and publishes (a) the state the markup needs to render and (b) prop getters - functions that return the attributes, ids, refs and handlers a consumer must spread onto the corresponding element, composing rather than replacing anything the consumer supplies. The call site renders from that state and feeds events back through the getters' handlers; re-rendering happens because the host runtime re-runs the consumer's render step when the state changes, so where no such runtime exists the consumer must be told to repaint explicitly. Keep the state machine testable on its own and make misuse loud (getter used on the wrong element, required part missing), because the markup half of the contract now lives in the consumer's code.
code_sketch:
primitive = disclosure(default_expanded=False)   # behaviour: owns state + transitions
props = primitive.getters()                       # prop getters: what the markup must spread

# consumer-supplied markup:
render(button(props["trigger"], content="Details"),
       panel(props["panel"], visible=primitive.state.expanded))

# events arrive through the getters' handlers and move the state machine
pitfalls: Skipping the getters and letting the consumer read internal state directly recreates the coupling the pattern removes - the primitive can no longer change its internals.
Publishing a mutable state object the consumer writes to makes the invariants unenforceable; publish state plus explicit transition functions.
Forgetting that the consumer now owns the DOM: without an accessibility contract and tests, the markup half silently breaks keyboard and screen-reader behaviour.

Controlled open state without onClose/onChange: creating a headless dialog or menu with a controlled isOpen but no escape hatch causes the primitive to appear read-only; the consumer must wire the escape key and outside-click to a state setter that matches the prop.

Manually adding ARIA attributes that the primitive already manages: manually setting aria-expanded, aria-controls or aria-activedescendant on top of a headless getter silently duplicates or overrides the primitive's own wiring, confusing screen readers without any console warning.

Rendering children both as render-prop and as regular children: some primitives support both a render-prop child and a regular children prop, which can cause the primitive to render twice per state change, producing double event handlers, double focus movement and double state updates.

Wrapping a headless primitive in a custom component without forwardRef or the proper 'as' polymorphism: focus management and ref forwarding break, and the consumer loses the ability to pass the root element type through, breaking layout and accessibility semantics.

Overriding built-in focus trapping (e.g. Dialog's focus trap) with an external focus-trap library: the two traps conflict, causing focus to cycle between the two libraries' intercepts or trap the user in an unexpected region.

Bundle size from multiple framework adapters: shipping one framework-free core plus per-framework adapters (React, Vue, Angular, Solid) in a single npm package without proper bundler splitting means every consumer pays for all adapters even if they use only one; use separate entry-points (headless-core, headless-react, headless-vue) and document which to import.

State machine actions that are not deterministic: if an action handler reads from the DOM (e.g. bounding rect), from a timer, or from a random value to compute the next state, the machine becomes hard to test in isolation and unpredictable under CI; move all non-determinism to side effects that are dispatched after the state transition, not into it.

Breaking the controlled/uncontrolled contract: a headless component that accepts isOpen (controlled) but internally also maintains its own open state — and the two diverge — produces a UI that is visually open but the primitive thinks is closed, breaking aria-expanded, focus restoration, and animation triggers simultaneously; the getter must always prefer the controlled value and fall back to internal state only when the prop is undefined.

Missing escape hatch for imperative focus: when a headless dialog opens, focus must move to the first focusable element; if the consumer renders a custom element as the 'first focusable' but it is not in the primitive's focus sequence (because it uses a non-standard element or a contenteditable), focus silently lands on the wrong element — expose a data attribute or aria-label that documents the expected first-focus target.

Over-composing primitives: stacking a headless Menu inside a headless Dialog inside a headless Tooltip creates a focus-tree that must be explicitly managed across all three layers; without a shared focus scope, Escape in the innermost layer closes all three instead of just the tooltip, confusing users who expect incremental dismissal.

TypeScript inference failures on prop getters: when prop getters return a union type (e.g. ButtonProps | InputProps depending on an options argument), TypeScript's inference degrades and consumers receive unknown instead of the concrete shape; solve with function overloads or a single branded return type rather than a union of getter return shapes.

Accessibility contract not tested in CI: a headless primitive with 100% unit test coverage on its state machine can still ship a broken ARIA contract if the composed examples are only tested manually; axe-core must run on every example story in CI, and the build must fail on accessibility violations at the same severity level as a unit test failure.

Wrong move: treating 'fully accessible' branding as a guarantee -> primitives built on div elements with an ARIA layer on top behave inconsistently across assistive technologies and add abstraction cost -> prefer primitives built on the native semantic element with ARIA only as augmentation, and verify with real screen readers rather than only axe checks.

Wrong move: choosing a headless library on API ergonomics alone -> accessibility-heavy behaviour cores silently add tens of kB gzipped (measured audits of the same 12-component app show a ~42 kB gzip spread between popular bases) and blow mobile budgets -> profile the per-component payload before adopting a primitive set.

Wrong move: rendering portal-based headless primitives (Dialog, Tooltip, Dropdown) inside a Shadow DOM web component -> the portal escapes the shadow root so the component's styles and z-index layering no longer apply -> either use the non-portal variant or accept a global stylesheet instead of shadow encapsulation.
